content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with sauce (NFS) is a ready‑to‑eat meal consisting of cooked pasta coated with a tomato‑based sauce seasoned with herbs and sometimes cheese. The product is designed for quick preparation of a hot lunch or dinner, requiring only heating in a microwave or on the stove.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The NFS (New Food Solutions) brand focuses on convenient semi‑finished foods for home and office use.
The pasta is usually made from durum wheat, giving it a firm texture after cooking.
The sauce is typically enriched with tomato paste, basil, oregano, and a touch of olive oil.
Some packages include a small amount of dried parmesan flakes for sprinkling before serving.
Vacuum packaging and preservative agents give the product a long shelf life.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides sustained energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Durum wheat offers plant‑based protein that can contribute to daily protein needs.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Most of the fat comes from plant sources, making it more heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Pasta provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce may be salty; individuals monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives used to extend shelf life may not be suitable for some sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While convenient, the meal can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in the microwave (about 3‑4 minutes) or on the stove, stir, and optionally add grated cheese, fresh herbs, or vegetables. Serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 2‑3 days and keep refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato skins are dried and roasted pieces of potato peel obtained from selected NFS (New Fresh Selection) varieties. They have a crunchy texture, a light salty taste, and the aroma of fresh potatoes. Used as a snack, ingredient in salads, soups, and various culinary dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato peel contains more fiber than the flesh.
Low‑temperature drying preserves most vitamins and minerals.
NFS potato skins are popular in vegetarian and vegan recipes as a crunchy breadcrumb substitute.
In some countries, potato peel is used as a source of dietary fiber in health foods.
When stored properly, they stay crisp for up to 12 months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium aids normal heart function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack foods, potato skins have little fat when not fried in oil.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in the peel help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to potato.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salted, the skins can be high in sodium, which may be a concern for some individuals.

items.title: Glycoalkaloids
items.content: Improperly processed peels may contain glycoalkaloids, which are toxic in large amounts.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small pieces can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Potato skins can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a crunchy topping for yogurts and porridge. They can also be crushed and used as a breadcrumb alternative in casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the skins in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Scrapple is a traditional American dish made from ground pork, liver, fat, and spices, formed into a loaf, sliced, and pan‑fried. Cooked scrapple has a firm texture, a savory flavor with hints of pepper and a subtle smokiness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scrapple originated in colonial America as a way to use leftover pork trimmings after a hog was slaughtered.
It is commonly served with maple syrup, apple sauce, or fried eggs.
In Pennsylvania, scrapple is considered a regional delicacy and often appears on breakfast menus.
There are many recipe variations: some add cornmeal or oats, others rely solely on meat and liver.
Scrapple is sometimes compared to British haggis, though the taste and texture differ.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Scrapple provides a substantial amount of animal protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: The liver component supplies iron, which is important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Scrapple contains vitamin B12 and B6, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc in scrapple contributes to immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Its fat content makes scrapple a calorie‑rich food that can provide lasting satiety.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Scrapple is rich in saturated fats, so people with cardiovascular concerns should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Recipes often include salt, which may be problematic for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to pork.

items.title: Liver toxins
items.content: Liver can contain trace toxins; using fresh, high‑quality ingredients reduces this risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Scrapple is typically sliced thin, then pan‑fried until crisp and golden. Serve hot with maple syrup, fried eggs, mashed potatoes, or as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked scrapple in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portioned bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before eating.

taco-or-tostada-salad-with-meat-and-sour.title: Taco or Tostada Salad with Meat and Sour Cream

content.title: About
content.content: Taco or tostada salad with meat and sour cream is a Mexican-inspired dish that combines crunchy tostada shells or soft tortilla rounds, fresh vegetables, aromatic spices, sautéed meat (usually beef or chicken), and a generous dollop of sour cream. It can be served cold or slightly warm, often accompanied by guacamole, salsa, and a wedge of lime.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A tostada is a fried corn tortilla that becomes a crisp base, popular in central Mexico.
Traditional taco meat is often grilled (asado) with chili, cumin, and oregano for a smoky flavor.
Sour cream adds a creamy tang, though some Mexican recipes use a lime‑infused crema instead.
The dish is commonly garnished with fresh cilantro, radish slices, and avocado.
Taco shells can be soft corn tortillas or fried to a crunchy texture.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides complete, high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables supply B6, B12, and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Sour cream contributes calcium and phosphorus, important for bone strength.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes, bell peppers, and cilantro are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids that combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fresh veggies and the tostada shell add fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces or salted tostadas can raise the sodium level, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Sour cream and fried tostadas add saturated fats; those monitoring cholesterol should moderate portions.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Some tortillas contain wheat; choose gluten‑free options if you have celiac disease.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Meat must be cooked thoroughly to avoid salmonella or campylobacter risks.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Lay out crisp tostada shells or split tortilla rounds, top with a mix of diced vegetables (tomatoes, cucumber, red onion), add seasoned sautéed meat, drizzle with sour cream, and garnish with cilantro, avocado slices, and lime wedges. Serve alongside guacamole and salsa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep tostadas separate to stay crunchy. Keep sour cream tightly sealed and use within its expiration date.
